name: Shoji
tagline: A small native macOS utility sold directly as a Mac download, the kind that lives in the menu bar and does one thing to your screen.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified, and the licensing model (one-time vs subscription) was not confirmed.

verdictSummary: Single-purpose native Mac utilities are the most clonable category of paid software there is: a menu bar item, a window or an overlay, a hotkey, a preferences pane, and you are done. A coding agent that knows SwiftUI and AppKit will get you something that runs on your own machine in a sitting. What it will not get you is the part that makes a Mac app feel like a Mac app: correct behavior across multiple displays and Spaces, Screen Recording and Accessibility permission flows that do not break on every OS update, a signed and notarized build, and an icon you are not embarrassed by. Details of the shipped feature set were not verified at draft time, so treat this as a judgment on the shape of the app rather than a line-by-line comparison. Build it if you enjoy Xcode; buy it if your time has a dollar value.
coreLoopDIY: A SwiftUI menu bar app that toggles configurable full-screen or region overlay panels on and off with a global hotkey, with per-display settings persisted locally.
requirements: A Mac running a recent macOS
Xcode and an Apple ID for local signing
Willingness to grant Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions to your own unsigned build
whatYouLose: A signed, notarized, Gatekeeper-friendly build that opens without a right-click ritual
Sane behavior across multiple monitors, Spaces, and full-screen apps, which is where these apps actually earn their money
Auto-updates, so your build silently rots at the next macOS release
Design polish: icon, animations, preferences layout, the small stuff that is most of the product
Someone to email when macOS changes a window-server API out from under you
moatNotes: The moat on indie Mac utilities is almost entirely taste plus the maintenance treadmill of annual OS releases.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a one-off Mac app costs about what one hour of your time costs, and it keeps working after the next OS update without you reopening Xcode. The value is not the feature, it is that someone else has already hit every multi-display, permissions, and sandbox edge case and will hit the next batch too. Your clone is a toy until you have fought the window server for a weekend, and then it is a chore.
notes: Verdict is on the category shape, not a verified feature-by-feature teardown; the exact shipped behavior was not confirmed.
prompt:
Build a native macOS menu bar utility in Swift using SwiftUI and AppKit. Xcode project, no third-party packages, no accounts, no network calls, no telemetry.

What it does:
- Lives only in the menu bar: LSUIElement = true, no Dock icon, no main window.
- Menu bar icon toggles an overlay on and off.
- The overlay is one borderless NSWindow per connected display, at a high window level, click-through optional, that covers either the full screen or a user-defined rectangle.
- Overlay appearance is configurable: solid color with opacity, or an NSVisualEffectView blur.
- A global hotkey toggles the overlay. Default is Control + Option + S, remappable in preferences.

Preferences window (SwiftUI, opened from the menu):
- Color picker, opacity slider, blur on/off.
- Full screen vs region, with a drag-to-select region picker per display.
- Hotkey recorder.
- Launch at login via SMAppService.
- Persist everything in UserDefaults. No config files, no cloud sync.

Correctness requirements, do not skip these:
- Handle display connect and disconnect by rebuilding overlay windows on NSApplication.didChangeScreenParametersNotification.
- Set collectionBehavior so overlays follow across Spaces and appear over full-screen apps where macOS allows it.
- Explain in the README which overlays macOS will refuse to draw over, instead of pretending it works everywhere.

Out of scope: screenshots, recording, iCloud sync, licensing, updates, analytics, an installer.

Deliver: a buildable Xcode project, a README with build and local-signing steps, and a short list of the permission prompts the user should expect on first run.
